card.intuition: A read-heavy catalog fronted by a searchable, cached inventory, connected to a cart service that holds line items, and an order service that turns a cart into an order through idempotent checkout. Inventory is decremented on checkout, and the whole flow is decoupled with a message queue so order fulfillment can lag behind placement.
card.analogy: A department store: shoppers browse shelves (catalog + inventory screens) with many lookers and few buyers, fill a shopping cart, and take it to the register where the exact items are locked in an order and handed to the stockroom to pick and ship.
card.time_complexity: Browsing and cart ops are O(1) per item with caching; checkout is O(items) plus the contended inventory decrement.
card.space_complexity: Catalog, per-user carts, and orders each scale with their own volume; hot SKUs need careful inventory modeling.
when_to_use: Building an online storefront with a huge catalog and read-heavy traffic
Modeling multi-step checkout where inventory and payment must stay consistent
Async order processing (pick, pack, ship, notify) decoupled from the customer-facing checkout
gotchas: Inventory must never go negative on checkout — decrement under a conditional/atomic update
A cart is not an order: checkout must be idempotent so retries don't create duplicate orders
Catalog read traffic dwarfs writes; pessimistically scaling the DB for writes wastes resources

steps.annotation: Shoppers browse the catalog and add items to their cart.
Catalog lookups are served from a search index and cache to absorb read traffic.
Cart line items accumulate per user without touching inventory yet.
Checkout atomically decrements inventory and creates an order idempotently.
Order placement fans out to a queue for pick, pack, ship, and notifications.

exercise.prompt: Inventory has 120 units of an item. Checkout decrements inventory by the quantity sold. After three orders of 5, 20, and 10, how many units remain?
exercise.starter_code:
inventory = 120
demands = [5, 20, 10]

remaining = inventory - sum(demands)
# Result is ___ units
hints: Sum the sold quantities and subtract from starting inventory
